citations.quote: Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by $$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$ The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define $$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$ using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $h:Q\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Then $h$ is differentiable almost everywhere, its partial derivatives are measurable and are its weak derivatives. On every open region where $h$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $|Dh|\le L$ almost everywhere. Let $H^m$ denote the repository's unnormalised Hausdorff measure, put $c_m=H^m((0,1]^m)$, and write $\sigma_m=c_m^{-1}H^m$ also on Euclidean spaces containing $m$-dimensional subsets. The graph map $F(y)=(y,h(y))$ satisfies, for every nonnegative Borel $a$,
$$\int_{F(Q)}a(x)\,d\sigma_m(x)=\int_Qa(F(y))\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}\,dy.$$
For the epigraph $G=\{(y,z):y\in Q,\ z>h(y)\}$, a smooth vector field compactly supported away from the chart sides satisfies
$$\int_G\operatorname{div}\phi\,dx=\int_Q\phi(y,h(y))\cdot(Dh(y),-1)\,dy.$$
Thus its outward normal is $(Dh,-1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ almost everywhere. The sign reverses for a subgraph. The graph surface measure is locally finite and Radon on $F(Q)$ with its relative topology, and its null sets coincide with graph images of Lebesgue-null subsets of the base.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable $f : V \to [0,\infty]$, $$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then $$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. derivations.claim: Put $B=B(0,1)$ and first prove its flux formula directly from [F2]. Cover $\partial B$ by finitely many graph neighborhoods, each expressing $B$ locally as an epigraph or subgraph of a smooth function, and add an interior open set compactly contained in $B$ to cover $\overline B$. Rigid changes of coordinates preserve volume, divergence and normal flux by [F3]–[F5], so the graph identities apply in these coordinates. Choose smooth nonnegative functions $\eta_i$ compactly supported in those sets and with $\sum_i\eta_i>0$ on $\overline B$: finitely many smaller balls cover this compact set, and ordinary Euclidean smooth bumps positive on those balls supply the functions. Normalize their sum on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, using one additional smooth cutoff equal to one near $\overline B$ and supported where that sum is positive. This gives functions $\chi_i$ subordinate to the same sets with $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ near $\overline B$. For any smooth compactly supported vector field $\psi$, apply [F2] to $\chi_i\psi$ in each boundary graph patch. Its divergence integral over $B$ is its outward flux over $\partial B$ by [F4], because the graph domain and $B$ agree on the support. The interior piece has divergence integral zero: its support is compact inside $B$, so choose a horizontal line below that support and apply [F2] on the half-plane above that line. The field vanishes on the line and its half-plane integral equals its whole-space integral, which equals its integral over $B$. Summing the finitely many identities, the derivatives of the partition cancel since its sum is one near $\overline B$. Consequently $\int_B\operatorname{div}\psi=\int_{\partial B}\psi\cdot\nu_B\,d\mathcal H^1$. This proves the required unit-disk identity without using a B-example or a stronger-choice divergence theorem.

Let $T(y)=x_0+ry$ and, for arbitrary $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$, put $\psi=\phi\circ T$. By [F5], $\operatorname{div}_y\psi(y)=r\,\operatorname{div}_x\phi(T(y))$. Applying [F3] to the positive and negative parts of $\operatorname{div}\phi$, whose integrals are finite because $\phi$ is smooth and compactly supported, gives
$$\int_E\operatorname{div}\phi(x)\,dx=r^2\int_B\operatorname{div}\phi(T(y))\,dy=r\int_B\operatorname{div}\psi(y)\,dy.$$
By step 1.1 this is $r\int_{\partial B}\psi\cdot
u_B\,d\mathcal H^1$. The circle parametrization in [F4] has outward normal $(\cos	heta,\sin	heta)$ and arclength element $r\,d	heta$, so this last expression equals $\int_{\partial E}\phi\cdot
u_E\,d\mathcal H^1$. Thus $\int_E\operatorname{div}\phi=\int_{\partial E}\phi\cdot
u_E\,d\mathcal H^1$ for every test field; [F1] yields $D\chi_E=-
u_E\mathcal H^1|_{\partial E}$.

By [F4], the circle is parametrized with speed $r$, so $\mathcal H^1(\partial E)=2\pi r$. For any Borel partition $(A_j)$ of $\partial E$, [F1] and $|\nu_E|=1$ give $\sum_j|D\chi_E(A_j)|=\sum_j|\int_{A_j}\nu_E\,d\mathcal H^1|\le2\pi r$. For the reverse bound, partition the circle into $N$ equal arcs and their finitely many endpoints. The endpoints have zero arclength; on each arc, direct integration of $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)r$ gives a vector of norm $2r\sin(\pi/N)$. Thus the partition sum is $2rN\sin(\pi/N)$, which tends to $2\pi r$ as $N\to\infty$. By the partition definition in [F1], $TV(\chi_E;\mathbb R^2)=2\pi r$. This finite variation proves $\chi_E\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$.
Because $\overline E\subset D$, the full derivative measure in step 1.2 is supported inside $D$. Hence $TV(\chi_E;D)=|D\chi_E|(D)=|D\chi_E|(\mathbb R^2)=2\pi r$.
